judging_guidelines: Score only what is explicitly stated; do not infer capabilities or intentions.
Penalize vague fluff, buzzwords, and over-claims.
Do not reward verbosity; concise and clear beats long and padded.
Evaluate trigger terms as: 'would a user naturally say this when they need this skill?'
A missing 'Use when...' clause or equivalent explicit trigger guidance should cap completeness at 3.
Descriptions must use third person voice ('Processes files', 'Analyzes data'). Penalize first person ('I can help') or second person ('You can use this') by reducing specificity score by 1.

BOUNDARY GUIDANCE: Use odd scores (1, 3, 5) when the description clearly matches one anchor. Use even scores (2, 4) when it falls between two anchors. A score of 2 means noticeably below the midpoint; 4 means noticeably above it.

ANTI-DRIFT: After assigning each score, re-read the anchors for the score above and below. If the description fits a neighboring anchor better, adjust the score to whichever anchor is the best fit. This prevents anchoring bias in either direction.

TWO DESCRIPTION CLASSES: before scoring activation path, decide which class the skill is in. A description that states it is dispatched programmatically by a named orchestrator is a WORKER; score it on the completeness of that dispatch contract and never on natural-keyword coverage. Absence of user-intent keywords in a worker is the correct design and must not be scored as a gap. Everything else is USER-TRIGGERED; score it on natural-keyword coverage exactly as before.

Never recommend adding user-intent trigger keywords to a skill that declares a dispatch contract. That change makes the worker activate outside its pipeline, which is a correctness regression, not a discoverability improvement.
good_overall_examples: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents. Use when working with PDF files or when the user mentions PDFs, forms, or document extraction.
Analyze Excel spreadsheets, create pivot tables, generate charts. Use when analyzing Excel files, spreadsheets, tabular data, or .xlsx files.
Generate descriptive commit messages by analyzing git diffs. Use when the user asks for help writing commit messages or reviewing staged changes.

Presentation creation, editing, and analysis. When Claude needs to work with presentations (.pptx files) for: (1) Creating new presentations, (2) Modifying or editing content, (3) Working with layouts, (4) Adding comments or speaker notes, or any other presentation tasks.

Applies Anthropic's official brand colors and typography to any sort of artifact that may benefit from having Anthropic's look-and-feel. Use it when brand colors or style guidelines, visual formatting, or company design standards apply.

dimensions.name: Specificity of Capabilities
dimensions.question: Does it describe concrete actions vs vague language?

scores.anchor: Entirely vague; no concrete actions; pure abstract language
scores.example: Helps with documents

scores.anchor: Names the domain but actions are minimal or generic
scores.example: Processes PDF files

scores.anchor: Names domain and 1-2 concrete actions, but not comprehensive
scores.example: Processes PDF files and extracts content

scores.anchor: Lists several specific actions; minor gaps in coverage
scores.example: Extracts text from PDF files, fills forms, converts pages to images

scores.anchor: Lists multiple specific concrete actions; comprehensive coverage
scores.example: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents, convert pages to images

dimensions.name: Activation Path Clarity
dimensions.question: Can a reader tell exactly how this skill is meant to be activated, and does the description serve that activation path?

scores.anchor: The activation path is unreadable, or the description actively serves the wrong one: a worker that is dispatched by name carries user-intent trigger phrasing, inviting the unanchored run.
scores.example: A pipeline worker described as 'Use when you want to analyze a legacy codebase' - user phrasing on a skill its orchestrator invokes by exact name, so any user mentioning legacy code fires it with no pipeline state.

scores.anchor: Activation path only guessable. A user-triggered skill offers one or two generic keywords; or a dispatched worker states no dispatch contract and merely lacks keywords, so its low keyword count reads as an oversight.
scores.example: 'Works with files' - or a worker whose description names its outputs but never says who calls it.

scores.anchor: Activation path inferable but under-specified. A user-triggered skill has relevant keywords but misses common variations; or a dispatched worker names its orchestrator without naming its predecessor or its direct-invocation escape hatch.
scores.example: 'Works with PDF files' - or 'Dispatched by the orchestrator.' with no predecessor and no resume path.

scores.anchor: Activation path explicit and well served, with a gap. A user-triggered skill has good keyword coverage missing a few natural terms; or a dispatched worker states the contract but omits the NOT-for clauses that keep it distinct from its siblings.
scores.example: 'PDF files, forms, document extraction' - or a dispatch contract naming orchestrator and predecessor but no disambiguation.

scores.anchor: Activation path unambiguous and fully served for its class. User-triggered: comprehensive natural terms including synonyms and file extensions. Dispatched: an explicit contract naming the orchestrator, the predecessor phase, and the direct-invocation path reserved for resume/debug, plus NOT-for disambiguation - and deliberately no user-intent keywords, which is correct here, not a gap.
scores.example: 'Dispatched programmatically by <orchestrator> after <predecessor> - never auto-triggered by user phrasing; direct "/<name>" is for resume/debug. NOT for <sibling's job>.'

dimensions.rationale: A skill is reachable by one of two paths, and they want opposite descriptions. A user-triggered skill is found by phrasing, so it needs the words a user would actually say. An orchestrator-dispatched worker is invoked by exact name by its parent, so user-intent keywords are not merely useless there - they cause the worker to fire outside its pipeline, with no anchor state and its ordering gates silently no-ops. Scoring both classes on natural-keyword coverage alone rewards the change that breaks the second class.

dimensions.name: Completeness
dimensions.question: Does it explicitly answer both 'what does this do' AND 'when should Claude use it'?

scores.anchor: Missing both what and when, or both are extremely vague
scores.example: Helps with documents

scores.anchor: Has a vague 'what' and no 'when'; or only 'when' is present without 'what'
scores.example: Use when working with documents

scores.anchor: Has a clear 'what' but 'when' is missing or only weakly implied
scores.example: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents

scores.anchor: Has both 'what' and 'when'; 'when' could be more explicit or specific
scores.example: Extract text from PDFs and fill forms. Use when working with PDF files.

scores.anchor: Clearly and explicitly answers both what AND when with concrete trigger phrases
scores.example: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents. Use when working with PDF files or when the user mentions PDFs, forms, or document extraction.

dimensions.name: Distinctiveness / Conflict Risk
dimensions.question: Is it clearly distinguishable from other skills; unlikely to trigger for the wrong skill?

scores.anchor: Entirely generic; would conflict with virtually any skill
scores.example: Helps with code and documents

scores.anchor: Very broad; high overlap risk with many similar skills
scores.example: Helps with document files

scores.anchor: Somewhat specific but could still overlap with similar skills
scores.example: Works with document files

scores.anchor: Mostly distinct; minor overlap risk with closely related skills
scores.example: Works with PDF and Word document files

scores.anchor: Clear niche with distinct triggers; minimal conflict risk
scores.example: Extract text and tables from PDF files, fill forms, merge documents. Use when working with PDF files or when the user mentions PDFs.
